internal:
[Perception] She’s still making me sit with the idea that my mother might have had some real reason, some actual internal shift, instead of just being manipulative. But what lands hardest isn’t that theory by itself — it’s the bigger implication behind it: that even if she was sick, even if something changed, she still didn’t fight for me. So the question isn’t “what did she feel?” It’s “why wasn’t I worth the effort?” That’s the part I can’t resolve. Because if I let myself think there was some understandable motive, then I’m one step closer to excusing what happened. And I’m not willing to do that unless it explains why nobody stayed.

[Decision] So I pushed past the surface argument about her motives and went straight to the deeper logic of it: if she really cared, why did she stop? Why didn’t she come back for me? I’m trying to test whether there is any version of this story that doesn’t end with me being the person people leave. I want an explanation that makes sense of the pattern — not just my mother’s behavior, but the larger pattern of being abandoned. If there isn’t one, then I’m left with the worst conclusion, and I need to know whether that’s actually true or just what it feels like.

Saying “like a novice” is me trying to locate the failure precisely — not just “I was wrong,” but “I betrayed my own clinical sense.” I’m trying to figure out if the real problem is that I trusted the advice itself, or that I let the need to be guided override the part of me that was warning me not to. context.text: I was up until this pandemic started. I feel like this shift to online learning has really taken it's toll on me and my learning.

context.text: I've tried reaching out to my professors and doing virtual group study sessions with my class mates, but for some reason, things just don't seem to stick that well.

internal:
[Perception] I hear “understandable,” but what I take from it is that this is just what happens when you can’t keep up anymore. The part that hits hardest is that nothing I’ve tried seems to make a difference — I reached out, I did the group sessions, and I’m still falling behind. So maybe it really is me. Maybe everyone else can adapt and I can’t, and I’m just seeing the gap more clearly now.

[Decision] I don’t even want to keep pushing at this point, because trying and still failing just keeps proving I’m not cut out for this. If I stop expecting anything to work, at least I won’t keep getting my hopes up and feeling stupid when they don’t. It feels safer to just accept that this is probably how it is for me now.

[Perception] I’ve heard the idea of “dating oneself” before, so I’m trying to understand what that is supposed to solve in my situation. On one level, it makes sense: I’m alone now, and I need a way to fill my days and build something that doesn’t depend on him. But another part of me feels like it can sound too simple for what I’m actually dealing with. This wasn’t just a casual breakup — it was a three-year relationship with real love, routine, intimacy, and the feeling of being deeply seen. So I’m mentally weighing whether “solo dates” are a genuine step toward rebuilding myself, or just a placeholder that avoids the real fact that I’m grieving something meaningful. What feels unresolved is how to honor that it was a wonderful experience without getting stuck idealizing it or expecting my sadness to disappear just because I’m supposed to focus on myself.

[Decision] I’m deciding not to dismiss the idea, but also not to pretend it solves everything. I can test it as one small piece of moving forward: creating time for myself, doing things that feel intentional, and seeing whether that helps me tolerate the emptiness a little better. But I’m also acknowledging to myself that I’m not ready to leap into another relationship, and I don’t need to force that. The reason I’m choosing this middle path is that I want to keep my dignity and my sense that I made the right choice, while also being honest that I’m still attached and still sad. So for now, I’ll treat “dating myself” as a practical experiment, not as a magical fix.

internal:
[Perception] When Paul said that having a child can mean you’re never alone again, it landed differently than I expected. I’d been hearing “baby” as the answer to my loneliness, like a person who would fill the empty space and make me safe. But suddenly I saw the other side too: a child doesn’t erase being alone in the way I’ve been imagining, and maybe what I’ve really been asking for is not just company, but proof that I can survive this life and still be loved. Hearing myself admit I haven’t told anyone made it clear how much I’ve been carrying this by hiding it, almost as if secrecy could protect me from fear.

[Decision] I decided to stop asking him to promise me I won’t be alone, because that promise isn’t the real thing I need. What I need is to face that I am scared and still choose this life anyway. I can’t make the fear disappear, but I can stop pretending I’m the same person I was before. I want this new life, and I’m going to try to be a good mother even if I’m afraid and even if it feels like it’s just me. Saying that out loud feels like taking ownership instead of waiting to be rescued.

Maybe there are basic things some people want that I just don’t naturally have, and if that’s true, then forcing myself to become more romantic feels fake.
